q: At a clinic, the ratio of new patients to returning patients is 5:7. If 35 new patients came on Monday, how many more returning patients than new patients came?
w: One part = 35 ÷ 5 = 7 patients. Returning patients = 7 × 7 = 49. Difference: 49 - 35 = 14.

n.0: This is the number of returning patients, not how many more returning patients there were.
n.2: This finds 2/7 of 35, dividing by the returning term (7) instead of the new term (5) to get one part.
n.3: This subtracts the ratio terms (7 - 5). Each part stands for 7 patients, so the difference is 2 × 7 = 14.

q: Of the 30 students in a nursing assistant class, 18 passed the skills test on the first attempt. What is the ratio of students who passed to students who did not, in lowest terms?
w: Students who did not pass: 30 - 18 = 12. Passed to did not pass: 18:12. Divide both by 6: 3:2.

n.0: This compares those who passed with the whole class (18:30), a part-to-whole ratio.
n.1: This compares the whole class with those who passed (30:18).
n.2: This reverses the order: it compares students who did not pass with those who passed.

q: A $6,000 scholarship fund is divided among three nursing students in the ratio 2:3:5. How much does the student with the largest share receive?

n.1: This splits the fund equally three ways (6,000 ÷ 3). The shares follow the ratio 2:3:5.
n.2: This is the smallest share (2 parts), not the largest.
n.3: This is the middle share (3 parts), not the largest.

q: A unit has 12 RNs and 20 nursing assistants. How many RNs must be added so that the ratio of RNs to nursing assistants becomes 4:5?
w: With 20 nursing assistants, 5 parts = 20, so one part = 4. RNs needed: 4 × 4 = 16. RNs to add: 16 - 12 = 4.

n.0: This is the number of RNs needed in total, not the number to add.
n.2: This compares ratio terms: 12:20 is 3:5, and 4 - 3 = 1. Each part stands for 4 people, not 1.
n.3: This reverses the ratio, making RNs 5/4 of 20 (25), then subtracts 12.

q: A disinfectant is mixed using 1 part concentrate to 19 parts water. What percent of the mixture is concentrate? Round to the nearest tenth.
w: Total parts: 1 + 19 = 20. Concentrate: 1/20 = 0.05 = 5.0%.

n.0: This is the percent of the mixture that is water (19/20).
n.1: This divides 1 by 19, treating the part-to-part ratio as a fraction of the whole mixture.
n.3: This moves the decimal point only one place. 0.05 = 5.0%.

q: A pediatric unit has 3 nurses for every 8 patients. Which ratio compares the patients to all the people (nurses and patients) on the unit?
w: Each group of 3 nurses and 8 patients has 3 + 8 = 11 people. Patients to all people: 8:11.

n.0: This is patients to nurses, a part-to-part ratio. The question asks for patients to everyone.
n.1: This reverses the order: all people to patients.
n.3: This is nurses to all people. The question asks for patients first.

q: A patient takes 750 mg of a medication in the morning and 1.5 g at night. What is the ratio of the morning dose to the night dose, in lowest terms?
w: Match units first: 1.5 g = 1,500 mg. Morning to night: 750:1,500. Divide both by 750: 1:2.

n.0: This reverses the order. The morning dose is named first, so it comes first.
n.1: This converts 1.5 g to 15,000 mg. Grams to milligrams is × 1,000, so 1.5 g = 1,500 mg.
n.2: This divides 750 by 1.5 without converting grams to milligrams.

q: A baker mixes flour, sugar and butter in the ratio 5:2:3 by weight. She uses 12 ounces of sugar. How many ounces of butter does she use?
w: Sugar is 2 parts, so one part = 12 ÷ 2 = 6 ounces. Butter: 3 × 6 = 18 ounces.

n.1: This is the amount of flour (5 parts), not butter.
n.2: This scales the wrong way, multiplying 12 by 2/3 instead of by 3/2.
n.3: This is the total weight of all three ingredients (10 parts).

q: On a unit, the ratio of RNs to LPNs is 3:2 and the ratio of LPNs to aides is 4:5. What is the ratio of RNs to aides?
w: Make the LPN terms match: 3:2 = 6:4. Now RNs:LPNs:aides = 6:4:5, so RNs to aides = 6:5.

n.0: This joins the outer terms of the two ratios without first making the LPN terms equal.
n.2: This multiplies across the wrong terms (3 × 5 and 2 × 4).
n.3: This reverses the order: aides to RNs.

q: A pharmacy sells the same brand of vitamin gummies in four bottle sizes. Which bottle has the lowest price per gummy?
w: Unit price = price ÷ quantity. $6.08 ÷ 32 = $0.19 per gummy, the lowest of $0.21, $0.19, $0.205, and $0.22.

n.0: $5.04 ÷ 24 = $0.21 per gummy, which is more than $0.19.
n.1: This is the largest bottle, but $8.20 ÷ 40 = $0.205 per gummy, which is more than $0.19.
n.2: This has the lowest total price, but $3.52 ÷ 16 = $0.22 per gummy, the highest unit price.

q: A patient in a weight-management program weighed 182 pounds at week 2 and 173 pounds at week 6. On average, how many pounds per week did the patient lose over this period?
w: Weight lost: 182 - 173 = 9 pounds. Time: week 2 to week 6 is 6 - 2 = 4 weeks. Rate: 9 ÷ 4 = 2.25 pounds per week.

n.0: This divides the 9-pound loss by 6, the week number, instead of the 4 weeks that passed.
n.2: This divides the 9-pound loss by 2, the starting week number, instead of the 4 weeks that passed.
n.3: This divides the weeks by the pounds (4 ÷ 9), which inverts the rate.

q: Ava drove 168 miles to a nursing school open house in 3 hours 30 minutes. What was her average speed for the drive?
w: 3 hours 30 minutes = 3.5 hours. Speed = distance ÷ time = 168 ÷ 3.5 = 48 miles per hour.

n.0: This rounds the time up to 4 hours before dividing.
n.1: This reads 3 hours 30 minutes as 3.30 hours. Thirty minutes is 0.5 hour, so the time is 3.5 hours.
n.2: This divides by 3 hours and ignores the extra 30 minutes.

q: A home health nurse drives 30 miles to a patient's home at an average of 60 miles per hour and returns along the same route at an average of 40 miles per hour. What is her average speed for the whole round trip?
w: Time out: 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5 hour. Time back: 30 ÷ 40 = 0.75 hour. Total: 60 miles in 1.25 hours, so 60 ÷ 1.25 = 48 miles per hour.

n.1: This uses the slower return speed as if it applied to the whole trip.
n.2: This divides the one-way distance of 30 miles by the total time of 1.25 hours.
n.3: This averages the two speeds. Average speed is total distance ÷ total time, and more time is spent at the slower speed.

q: An IV of 1,500 mL is ordered to infuse over 12 hours. After 5 hours, 700 mL have infused. At what rate must the rest of the IV run so that it finishes on time? Round to the nearest whole number.
w: Volume left: 1,500 - 700 = 800 mL. Time left: 12 - 5 = 7 hours. Rate = 800 ÷ 7 = 114.29, which rounds to 114 mL per hour.

n.0: This divides the remaining 800 mL by the 5 hours already used instead of the 7 hours left.
n.2: This is the rate so far, 700 ÷ 5, not the rate needed for the remaining volume.
n.3: This is the original rate, 1,500 ÷ 12. The IV is ahead of schedule (700 mL infused instead of 625 mL), so 125 mL per hour for 7 more hours would deliver 1,575 mL and finish early.

q: A medical assistant counts 23 heartbeats in 20 seconds. At this rate, what is the patient's heart rate in beats per minute? Enter the number of beats per minute.

tr.46: Doubled the 20-second count instead of tripling it.
tr.1.15: Divided 23 by 20 to get beats per second and stopped.

w: One minute is 60 seconds, which is 3 × 20 seconds. Heart rate = 23 × 3 = 69 beats per minute.

q: A tablet used for charting shows 92% battery at 1:15 p.m. and 64% battery at 4:45 p.m. What is the average rate at which the battery charge decreased, in percentage points per hour? Enter the number only.

tr.8.48: Wrote 3 hours 30 minutes as 3.3 hours instead of 3.5 hours.

w: Change: 92 - 64 = 28 percentage points. Time: 1:15 p.m. to 4:45 p.m. = 3 hours 30 minutes = 3.5 hours. Rate = 28 ÷ 3.5 = 8 percentage points per hour.

q: Pharmacy A fills 135 prescriptions in 9 hours. Pharmacy B fills 48 prescriptions in 2 hours 40 minutes. How many more prescriptions per hour does Pharmacy B fill than Pharmacy A?
w: Pharmacy A: 135 ÷ 9 = 15 per hour. Pharmacy B: 2 hours 40 minutes = 2 2/3 hours = 160 minutes; 48 ÷ 160 = 0.3 per minute × 60 = 18 per hour. Difference: 18 - 15 = 3.

n.1: This reads 2 hours 40 minutes as 2.4 hours, giving 48 ÷ 2.4 = 20 per hour for Pharmacy B.
n.2: This is Pharmacy B's rate, not the difference between the two rates.
n.3: This is Pharmacy A's rate, not the difference between the two rates.

q: An IV delivers 390 mL in 3 hours 15 minutes. At this rate, how many milliliters are delivered per hour? Round to the nearest tenth.
w: 15 minutes = 15/60 = 0.25 hour, so the time is 3.25 hours. Rate = 390 ÷ 3.25 = 120.0 mL per hour.

n.0: This reads 3 hours 15 minutes as 3.15 hours. Fifteen minutes is 0.25 hour.
n.2: This rounds the time up to 4 hours before dividing.
n.3: This divides by 3 hours and leaves out the 15 minutes.

q: A pharmacy technician fills 18 prescriptions every 45 minutes. At this rate, how long will it take to fill 60 prescriptions?
w: Time per prescription: 45 ÷ 18 = 2.5 minutes. For 60: 60 × 2.5 = 150 minutes = 2 hours 30 minutes.

n.0: This finds 2.5 hours and reads the 0.5 as 50 minutes. Half an hour is 30 minutes.
n.1: This divides 60 by 18 (3.33) and treats the result as hours. The 18 prescriptions take 45 minutes, not 1 hour.
n.2: This writes 150 minutes as 1 h 50 min. An hour has 60 minutes, so 150 minutes = 2 h 30 min.

q: Which package of the same brand of oatmeal has the lowest price per ounce? (1 pound = 16 ounces)

n.1: $11.20 ÷ 32 ounces = $0.35 per ounce. Two pounds is 32 ounces, and $0.35 is still higher than $0.34.
n.2: $5.76 ÷ 16 ounces = $0.36 per ounce, higher than $0.34.
n.3: $4.44 ÷ 12 = $0.37 per ounce, the highest of the four.

q: An ambulance travels 42 miles in 35 minutes. What is its average speed in miles per hour?
w: 35 minutes = 35/60 hour. Speed = 42 ÷ (35/60) = 42 × 60 ÷ 35 = 72 miles per hour.

n.1: This treats 35 minutes as half an hour (42 ÷ 0.5).
n.2: This rounds 35/60 = 0.583 to 0.6 hour before dividing (42 ÷ 0.6). Round only at the end.
n.3: This writes 35 minutes as 0.35 hour. Thirty-five minutes is 35/60 of an hour.

q: An infusion runs at 80 mL per hour from 9:30 a.m. to 3:45 p.m. How many milliliters are infused?
w: Elapsed time: 9:30 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. is 6 hours, plus 15 minutes = 6.25 hours. Volume: 80 × 6.25 = 500 mL.

n.0: This writes 6 hours 15 minutes as 6.15 hours. Fifteen minutes is 0.25 hour.
n.1: This counts the time as 5 hours 45 minutes (5.75 × 80). From 9:30 a.m. to 3:45 p.m. is 6 hours 15 minutes.
n.3: This uses 6 hours and leaves out the extra 15 minutes.

q: Solve the proportion 6/x = 15/40.
w: Cross-multiply: 15x = 6 × 40 = 240. Divide by 15: x = 16. Check: 6/16 = 0.375 and 15/40 = 0.375.

n.0: This multiplies 15 by 40 and divides by 6, pairing the wrong terms when cross-multiplying.
n.2: This uses addition: 15 is 9 more than 6, so it takes 9 from 40. Proportions scale by multiplying, not adding.
n.3: This flips the second ratio, solving 6/x = 40/15, which gives 40x = 90.

q: A nursing student reads 45 pages of a pharmacology textbook in 1 hour 15 minutes. At the same rate, how long will it take her to read 162 pages?
w: 1 hour 15 minutes = 75 minutes. Set up 45/75 = 162/t. Cross-multiply: 45t = 12,150, so t = 270 minutes = 4 hours 30 minutes.

n.1: This uses 1 hour instead of 1 hour 15 minutes for the 45 pages.
n.2: This finds 4.5 hours and then reads the 0.5 as 50 minutes. Half an hour is 30 minutes.
n.3: This writes 1 hour 15 minutes as 1.15 hours. Fifteen minutes is 0.25 hour.

q: At the same time of day, a nurse who is 5.5 feet tall casts a shadow 4 feet long, and a flagpole outside the hospital casts a shadow 18 feet long. How tall is the flagpole?
w: Height/shadow is the same for both: 5.5/4 = h/18. Cross-multiply: 4h = 99, so h = 24.75 feet.

n.0: This subtracts the 1.5-foot difference from the shadow length. Similar figures scale by multiplying.
n.1: This sets up the second ratio upside down, giving 4 × 18 ÷ 5.5.
n.3: This adds the 1.5-foot difference between the nurse's height and shadow. Similar figures scale by multiplying.

q: It takes 3 aides 8 hours to restock all of a hospital's supply rooms. Working at the same rate, how long would it take 4 aides to do the same job?
w: This is an inverse proportion: aides × hours stays constant. 3 × 8 = 24 aide-hours, so 4 aides need 24 ÷ 4 = 6 hours.

n.0: This treats the relationship as direct. More aides finish faster, so the time must decrease.
n.1: This divides the original 8 hours by 4 aides and ignores that the 8 hours was for 3 aides.
n.2: This subtracts 1 hour for the 1 extra aide. The total work, 24 aide-hours, stays the same.

q: Solve the proportion (x + 2)/9 = 4/6.
w: Cross-multiply: 6(x + 2) = 4 × 9 = 36. Divide by 6: x + 2 = 6. Subtract 2: x = 4. Check: 6/9 = 2/3 and 4/6 = 2/3.

n.0: This flips the second ratio, solving (x + 2)/9 = 6/4.
n.1: This cross-multiplies without distributing: 6x + 2 = 36 instead of 6(x + 2) = 36.
n.2: This uses addition: 9 is 3 more than 6, so it adds 3 to 4. Proportions scale by multiplying.

q: A survey at a health fair found that 7 of every 20 visitors had their blood pressure checked. If 1,260 people visited the fair, how many would be expected to have had their blood pressure checked?
w: Set up 7/20 = x/1,260. Cross-multiply: 20x = 8,820, so x = 441.

n.0: This divides 1,260 by 7 instead of multiplying by 7/20.
n.1: This is 1/20 of the visitors, the size of one part, not 7 parts.
n.2: This is the number expected not to have had a check (13 of every 20).

q: A printer in a clinic prints 18 pages in 45 seconds. At this rate, how many pages can it print in 4 minutes?
w: Convert first: 4 minutes = 240 seconds. Set up 18/45 = p/240. Cross-multiply: 45p = 4,320, so p = 96 pages.

n.0: This treats 18 pages as the number printed per minute, multiplying 18 by 4.
n.1: This divides 45 by 18 and multiplies by 4, which inverts the rate.
n.3: This mixes units, comparing 4 minutes with 45 seconds without converting 4 minutes to 240 seconds.

q: Nine gallons of gas cost $31.41. Which proportion can be used to find c, the cost of 14 gallons of gas at the same price per gallon?
w: Keep the same units in the same positions: 9 gallons/$31.41 = 14 gallons/c. Cross-multiplying gives 9c = 439.74, so c = $48.86.

n.0: This puts the second ratio upside down. Gallons over dollars must be matched with gallons over dollars.
n.1: This pairs $31.41 with 14 gallons, but $31.41 is the cost of 9 gallons.
n.2: This pairs 9 gallons with the unknown cost and 14 gallons with $31.41, mismatching the quantities.

q: A 12-ounce bag of coffee makes 45 cups. At the same rate, how many cups can be made from a 32-ounce bag? Enter the number of cups.

tr.65: Added the 20-ounce difference to 45 instead of scaling.
tr.8.53: Set up the second ratio upside down (12 × 32 ÷ 45).

w: Set up 12/45 = 32/c. Cross-multiply: 12c = 1,440, so c = 120 cups.

q: A patient-education poster is enlarged proportionally from a draft that is 8 inches wide and 10 inches tall. The poster is 26 inches wide. How tall is the poster? Enter the number of inches.

tr.28: Added the 18-inch increase in width to the height instead of scaling.
tr.20.8: Set up the ratio upside down (26 × 8 ÷ 10).

w: Set up width/height: 8/10 = 26/h. Cross-multiply: 8h = 260, so h = 32.5 inches.

q: Which pair of quantities is in an inverse proportion?
o: The miles driven and the gallons of gas used at a steady fuel economy
The hours worked and the pay earned at a fixed hourly wage
The number of nurses sharing a fixed workload and the hours it takes
The number of 250 mg tablets given and the total milligrams given
w: In an inverse proportion the product stays constant: doubling the number of nurses on a fixed workload halves the hours. The other pairs increase together (direct proportion).

n.0: Miles and gallons increase together at a constant rate, so this is a direct proportion.
n.1: Pay grows at a constant rate as hours increase, so this is a direct proportion.
n.3: Each extra tablet adds 250 mg, so the total grows with the count: a direct proportion.

q: A soup recipe that serves 6 people uses 2 1/4 cups of broth. How many cups of broth are needed to make the recipe serve 10 people?
w: Set up 2.25/6 = x/10. Cross-multiply: 6x = 22.5, so x = 3.75 = 3 3/4 cups.

n.0: This adds 4 cups for the 4 extra servings instead of scaling by 10/6.
n.2: This doubles the recipe, but 10 servings is 10/6 = 1 2/3 times the recipe, not 2 times.
n.3: This sets up the proportion upside down, multiplying 2 1/4 by 6/10.

q: On a state map, 1.5 inches represents 40 miles. Two towns are 5.25 inches apart on the map. What is the actual distance between the two towns?
w: Set up 1.5/40 = 5.25/d. Cross-multiply: 1.5d = 210, so d = 140 miles.

n.0: This rounds 26.67 miles per inch to 27 before multiplying. Round only at the end.
n.1: This multiplies 5.25 by 40 as if 1 inch represented 40 miles.
n.2: This multiplies 40 by 1.5 to get 60 miles per inch instead of dividing.

q: A cleaning solution for patient rooms is mixed using 3 ounces of concentrate for every 2 gallons of water. How many ounces of concentrate are needed for 4.5 gallons of water?
w: Set up 3/2 = x/4.5. Cross-multiply: 2x = 13.5, so x = 6.75 ounces.

n.1: This multiplies 3 ounces by 4.5 as if the 3 ounces were for 1 gallon.
n.2: This adds the extra 2.5 gallons to the 3 ounces instead of scaling.
n.3: This sets up the proportion upside down, multiplying 4.5 by 2/3.

q: A pancake recipe uses 1 1/2 cups of flour and 3/4 cup of milk. Kim has 2 cups of milk and wants to use all of it, keeping the same ratio of flour to milk. How many cups of flour does she need?
w: Flour/milk: 1.5/0.75 = x/2. The recipe uses 2 cups of flour per cup of milk (1.5 ÷ 0.75 = 2), so 2 × 2 = 4 cups of flour.

n.0: This sets up the ratio upside down, multiplying 2 by 3/4 and dividing by 1 1/2.
n.2: This multiplies 2 by 1 1/2 as if the 1 1/2 cups of flour went with 1 cup of milk.
n.3: This adds the extra 1 1/4 cups of milk to the flour instead of scaling.

q: An architect builds a model of a new hospital wing at a scale of 1:200. The model is 45 centimeters tall. How tall will the actual building be, in meters? (1 meter = 100 centimeters)
w: Each model centimeter represents 200 actual centimeters: 45 × 200 = 9,000 cm. Convert: 9,000 ÷ 100 = 90 meters.

n.0: This divides the model height by 200 instead of multiplying; the real building is larger than the model.
n.2: This divides 9,000 cm by 1,000 instead of 100; there are 100 cm in a meter.
n.3: This divides 9,000 cm by 10 instead of 100; there are 100 cm in a meter.

q: A punch recipe mixes 3 cups of juice with 5 cups of sparkling water. How many cups of juice are needed to make 14 cups of punch? Enter the number of cups.

tr.8.4: Used the part-to-part ratio 3/5 as the fraction of the punch that is juice.
tr.8.75: Found the amount of sparkling water instead of juice.

w: The recipe makes 3 + 5 = 8 cups, and 3 of those 8 cups are juice. Juice = 3/8 × 14 = 5.25 cups.

q: The scale on a trail map is 2 centimeters to 0.5 kilometer. A hike measures 13 centimeters on the map. What is the actual length of the hike?
w: Set up 2/0.5 = 13/d. Cross-multiply: 2d = 6.5, so d = 3.25 kilometers. (1 cm represents 0.25 km, and 13 × 0.25 = 3.25.)

n.1: This multiplies 13 by 2 and leaves out the 0.5 km.
n.2: This sets up the proportion upside down, multiplying 13 by 2 ÷ 0.5.
n.3: This multiplies 13 by 0.5 as if 1 cm represented 0.5 km; it is 2 cm that represents 0.5 km.

q: A provider orders amoxicillin 375 mg by mouth. The pharmacy supplies amoxicillin oral suspension containing 250 mg per 5 mL. How many milliliters should be given?
w: Desired ÷ have × quantity: 375 ÷ 250 × 5 = 1.5 × 5 = 7.5 mL. As a proportion: 250 mg/5 mL = 375 mg/x, so 250x = 1,875 and x = 7.5 mL.

n.1: This inverts the dose ratio, using 250/375 × 5 instead of 375/250 × 5.
n.2: This divides 375 mg by 5 mL, as if each milliliter held 5 mg.
n.3: This divides the desired dose by the dose on hand but does not multiply by the 5 mL quantity.

q: A medication is ordered at 15 mg per kilogram of body weight per day, divided into 3 equal doses. A child weighs 44 pounds. Using 1 kg = 2.2 lb, how many milligrams should be given in each dose?
w: Weight: 44 ÷ 2.2 = 20 kg. Daily dose: 15 × 20 = 300 mg. Each dose: 300 ÷ 3 = 100 mg.

n.0: This is the total daily dose; it must be divided into 3 equal doses.
n.2: This uses the weight in pounds and also gives a daily total, 44 × 15.
n.3: This uses the weight in pounds (44 × 15 ÷ 3) instead of converting to 20 kg first.

q: A provider orders heparin 7,500 units. The vial is labeled 5,000 units per mL. How many milliliters should be drawn up? Enter the number of milliliters.
w: Desired ÷ have × quantity: 7,500 ÷ 5,000 × 1 mL = 1.5 mL. As a proportion: 5,000 units/1 mL = 7,500 units/x, so x = 1.5 mL.

q: A provider orders 60 mg of a liquid medication every 6 hours. The medication is supplied as 20 mg per 5 mL. How many milliliters will the patient receive in 24 hours?
w: One dose: 60 ÷ 20 × 5 = 15 mL. Doses in 24 hours: 24 ÷ 6 = 4. Total: 4 × 15 = 60 mL.

n.0: This counts 5 doses by including both hour 0 and hour 24; every 6 hours gives 4 doses in a 24-hour day.
n.1: This is the volume for one dose; there are 24 ÷ 6 = 4 doses in 24 hours.
n.3: This multiplies one 15 mL dose by 24 as if a dose were given every hour.

q: A patient is to receive 0.6 mg of a medication per day, divided into 2 equal doses. Tablets contain 0.15 mg each. How many tablets are given per dose?
w: Each dose: 0.6 ÷ 2 = 0.3 mg. Desired ÷ have × quantity: 0.3 ÷ 0.15 × 1 = 2 tablets.

n.0: This is the number of tablets for the whole day (0.6 ÷ 0.15). The day's amount is split into 2 doses.
n.1: This is a decimal slip, dividing 0.3 by 0.015. Each tablet is 0.15 mg.
n.2: This inverts the ratio: 0.15 ÷ 0.3 = 0.5. Divide the desired dose by the dose on hand.

q: An order is for 0.45 g of a medication. The oral suspension contains 150 mg per 5 mL. How many milliliters should be given?
w: Convert: 0.45 g × 1,000 = 450 mg. Desired ÷ have × quantity: 450 ÷ 150 × 5 = 3 × 5 = 15 mL.

n.0: This inverts the ratio: 150 ÷ 450 × 5 = 1.7 mL.
n.1: This converts 0.45 g to 4,500 mg. Grams to milligrams is × 1,000, so 0.45 g = 450 mg.
n.2: This stops at desired ÷ have (450 ÷ 150 = 3) and does not multiply by the 5 mL quantity.

q: An order is for 125 mcg of a medication. Tablets on hand contain 0.25 mg each. How many tablets should be given? (1 mg = 1,000 mcg)
w: Convert: 125 mcg ÷ 1,000 = 0.125 mg. Desired ÷ have: 0.125 ÷ 0.25 = 0.5 tablet.

n.0: This converts 125 mcg to 0.0125 mg, moving the decimal point four places.
n.1: This inverts the ratio: 0.25 ÷ 0.125 = 2.
n.3: This converts 125 mcg to 1.25 mg, moving the decimal point only two places.

q: A provider orders 30 mg of a medication. The vial is labeled 40 mg per 2 mL. How many milliliters should be drawn up? Round to the nearest hundredth.
w: Desired ÷ have × quantity: 30 ÷ 40 × 2 = 0.75 × 2 = 1.50 mL.

n.1: This divides by the 2 mL quantity instead of multiplying: 0.75 ÷ 2.
n.2: This inverts the ratio: 40 ÷ 30 × 2 = 2.67 mL.
n.3: This stops at desired ÷ have (0.75) and does not multiply by the 2 mL quantity.

q: The prescribed amount of a medication is 4 mg per kilogram of body weight. A patient weighs 165 pounds. Using 1 kg = 2.2 lb, how many milligrams should be given?

n.1: This multiplies by 2.2 instead of dividing (165 × 2.2 × 4). Pounds to kilograms makes the number smaller.
n.2: This uses the weight in pounds (4 × 165) without converting to kilograms.
n.3: This is the weight in kilograms; it still has to be multiplied by 4 mg per kg.

q: A child who weighs 22 lb is prescribed 25 mg per kg. The liquid contains 125 mg per 5 mL. Using 1 kg = 2.2 lb, how many milliliters should be given?

n.0: This uses 22 lb as kilograms: 25 × 22 = 550 mg, then 550 ÷ 125 × 5 = 22 mL.
n.1: This stops at desired ÷ have (250 ÷ 125 = 2) and does not multiply by the 5 mL quantity.
n.3: This multiplies 22 by 2.2 instead of dividing, giving 48.4 kg and 48.4 mL.

q: An order is for 250 mg every 8 hours. Capsules contain 125 mg each. How many capsules are needed for 3 days?
w: Per dose: 250 ÷ 125 = 2 capsules. Doses per day: 24 ÷ 8 = 3. Per day: 2 × 3 = 6 capsules. For 3 days: 6 × 3 = 18 capsules.

n.0: This is the number of capsules for 1 day, not 3 days.
n.1: This counts 4 doses a day. Every 8 hours gives 24 ÷ 8 = 3 doses a day.
n.3: This is the number of doses in 3 days; each dose is 2 capsules.

q: An oral solution contains 80 mg of a medication in every 15 mL. How many milligrams are in 6 mL of the solution?
w: Set up mg over mL on both sides: 80/15 = x/6. Cross-multiply: 15x = 480, so x = 32 mg.

n.0: This is the amount in 1 mL (80 ÷ 15), not in 6 mL.
n.1: This divides the volumes by the dose (6 × 15 ÷ 80), mixing mL and mg positions.
n.2: This sets the proportion upside down (80 × 15 ÷ 6).

q: An order is for 45 mg. The label reads 30 mg per 2 mL. Which proportion can be solved to find x, the number of milliliters to give?
w: Keep mg over mL on both sides: 30 mg/2 mL = 45 mg/x mL. Cross-multiply: 30x = 90, so x = 3 mL.

n.0: This writes mL over mg on the left but mg over mL on the right, giving x = 675.
n.2: This pairs the ordered 45 mg with the 2 mL that holds 30 mg, giving x = 1.33.
n.3: This puts the second ratio upside down (mL over mg), giving x = 675.

q: An order is for 0.0375 g of a medication. Scored tablets contain 25 mg each. How many tablets should be given?
w: Convert: 0.0375 g × 1,000 = 37.5 mg. Desired ÷ have: 37.5 ÷ 25 = 1.5 tablets.

n.0: This converts 0.0375 g to 375 mg. Grams to milligrams is × 1,000, so 0.0375 g = 37.5 mg.
n.1: This converts 0.0375 g to 3.75 mg, moving the decimal point only two places.
n.2: This inverts the ratio: 25 ÷ 37.5 = 0.67.

q: A potassium supplement contains 20 mEq in every 15 mL. The order is for 30 mEq. How many milliliters should be given?
w: Desired ÷ have × quantity: 30 ÷ 20 × 15 = 1.5 × 15 = 22.5 mL.

n.0: This inverts the ratio: 20 ÷ 30 × 15 = 10 mL.
n.1: This stops at desired ÷ have and does not multiply by the 15 mL quantity.
n.2: This swaps the strength and the volume: 30 ÷ 15 × 20 = 40 mL.

q: A 120 mL bottle of liquid medication contains 250 mg per 5 mL. The dose is 500 mg twice a day. How many full days will the bottle last?
w: One dose: 500 ÷ 250 × 5 = 10 mL. Per day: 2 × 10 = 20 mL. Days: 120 ÷ 20 = 6 days.

n.0: This uses desired ÷ have (2) as the dose in mL, giving 4 mL per day.
n.1: This is the number of doses (120 ÷ 10), not days; there are 2 doses a day.
n.3: This inverts the ratio, giving 2.5 mL per dose and 5 mL per day.

q: A medication is ordered at 2 mg per minute. The solution contains 500 mg in 250 mL. At how many milliliters per hour should it run?
w: Strength: 500 mg ÷ 250 mL = 2 mg per mL. Per minute: 2 mg ÷ 2 mg per mL = 1 mL. Per hour: 1 × 60 = 60 mL per hour.

n.0: This is the rate per minute; there are 60 minutes in an hour.
n.1: This is the dose in milligrams per hour (2 × 60), not milliliters.
n.2: This inverts the strength, using 0.5 mg per mL (250 ÷ 500).

q: A patient who weighs 70 kg is prescribed 0.5 mg per kg per day, divided into 2 equal doses. How many milligrams are in each dose?
w: Daily amount: 0.5 × 70 = 35 mg. Each dose: 35 ÷ 2 = 17.5 mg.

n.1: This is the daily amount; it is divided into 2 doses.
n.2: This divides 70 by 0.5 instead of multiplying.
n.3: This multiplies the daily 35 mg by 2 instead of dividing it into 2 doses.

q: A rideshare driver is paid $3 for each trip plus $1.25 for every mile of the trip. Which expression gives the driver's pay, in dollars, for a single trip that is m miles long?
w: Total = fixed amount + rate × quantity. The fixed amount is $3 per trip and the rate is $1.25 per mile, so the pay is 1.25m + 3 dollars.

n.0: 1.25m and 3 are not like terms, so they cannot be combined; 4.25m would pay $4.25 for every mile.
n.1: This multiplies the $3 trip payment by 1.25 as well, which gives 1.25m + 3.75 instead of adding a flat $3.
n.3: This swaps the two amounts: $3 is the flat payment per trip, and $1.25 is the rate that multiplies the miles.

q: At a walk-in clinic, the number of evening appointments on Monday was 4 fewer than twice the number of morning appointments. If m is the number of morning appointments, which expression represents the number of evening appointments?
w: 'Twice the number of morning appointments' is 2m. '4 fewer than' that amount means subtract 4 from it: 2m - 4.

n.0: '4 fewer than' a quantity means 4 is subtracted from that quantity, so the 4 comes second; 4 - 2m reverses the order.
n.2: This swaps the numbers: the morning count is doubled (multiplied by 2), and then 4 is taken away.
n.3: This subtracts 4 before doubling, which equals 2m - 8, not 4 fewer than twice m.

q: What is the value of 3x² - 2xy + y when x = -2 and y = 5?
w: Substitute and follow the order of operations. 3x² = 3 × (-2)² = 3 × 4 = 12. -2xy = -2 × (-2) × 5 = +20. y = 5. Total: 12 + 20 + 5 = 37.

n.0: This squares 3x instead of x. 3x² means 3 × x² = 3 × 4 = 12, not (3 × -2)² = 36.
n.1: This misses a sign change: -2xy = -2 × (-2) × 5 = +20, not -20.
n.3: This treats x² as -4. Squaring a negative number gives a positive: (-2)² = 4, so 3x² = 12.

q: Which expression is equivalent to 4(2x - 3) - 3(x - 5)?
w: Distribute: 4(2x - 3) = 8x - 12 and -3(x - 5) = -3x + 15. Combine like terms: 8x - 3x = 5x and -12 + 15 = 3, so the expression is 5x + 3.

n.0: This distributes the 4 to 2x but not to -3. 4(2x - 3) = 8x - 12, not 8x - 3.
n.1: This multiplies only the x by -3 and then subtracts 5. The -3 must multiply both terms: -3(x - 5) = -3x + 15.
n.3: This multiplies -3 by -5 to get -15. A negative times a negative is positive, so -3(x - 5) = -3x + 15.

q: Which expression represents 'six less than the quotient of a number n and 4'?
w: 'The quotient of a number n and 4' is n/4. 'Six less than' that quotient subtracts 6 from it, so the expression is n/4 - 6.

n.0: 'Six less than' a quantity subtracts 6 from that quantity, so the quotient comes first: n/4 - 6, not 6 - n/4.
n.1: 'The quotient of n and 4' means n divided by 4. Writing 4/n reverses the division.
n.3: This subtracts 6 before dividing. The quotient n/4 is formed first, and then 6 is taken away.

q: A courier charges 3 times the sum of a package's weight w, in pounds, and 2, plus a $5 handling fee. Which expression gives the charge, in dollars, for one package?
w: 'The sum of w and 2' is (w + 2). '3 times the sum' is 3(w + 2). Adding the $5 handling fee gives 3(w + 2) + 5, which simplifies to 3w + 11.

n.0: This multiplies only w by 3. 'Times the sum' needs parentheses so both w and 2 are tripled: 3(w + 2) = 3w + 6.
n.1: This swaps the multiplier and the fee: the sum is multiplied by 3, and the $5 fee is then added.
n.2: This puts the $5 fee inside the parentheses, so the fee is tripled too. The fee is added once, after multiplying.

q: An urgent care clinic bills a $40 visit fee plus $25 for each lab test. A patient's bill came to $165. Which equation can be used to find t, the number of lab tests the patient had?
w: Total = fixed fee + rate × quantity, so 25t + 40 = 165. Solving: 25t = 125, so t = 5 lab tests.

n.0: The $40 fee is already part of the $165 bill, so it is subtracted from 165, not added: 25t = 165 - 40.
n.2: This multiplies the visit fee by 25 as well. The $40 is a one-time charge that is added to 25t.
n.3: This swaps the rate and the fixed fee: $25 is charged for each test, and $40 is charged once per visit.

q: A dietitian estimates a man's resting calorie needs with the expression 10w + 6.25h - 5a + 5, where w is weight in kilograms, h is height in centimeters, and a is age in years. What value does the expression give for w = 80, h = 175, and a = 40?

n.1: This leaves off the constant + 5 at the end of the expression.
n.2: This adds 5a instead of subtracting it: the expression has - 5a, so 200 is taken away.
n.3: This treats the final + 5 as - 5, which makes the result 10 lower.

q: A school nurse orders x boxes of bandages at $2.40 per box and x + 15 packs of gauze at $0.80 per pack. Which expression gives the total cost of the order, in dollars?

n.0: This adds the 15 extra packs without pricing them. The 15 packs cost 0.80 × 15 = $12.
n.2: This multiplies 15 by the combined price of 3.20. The extra 15 items are gauze packs, so 15 is multiplied by 0.80 only.
n.3: This misplaces the decimal point: 0.80 × 15 = 12, not 1.20.

q: If a = -3 and b = 4, what is the value of the expression 2a² + 5b - ab? Enter your answer as a number.

tr.68: Squared 2a instead of squaring a alone.

q: A home health agency pays its aides $22 per patient visit plus $0.67 for each mile driven between visits, so weekly pay is 22v + 0.67m dollars. How much does an aide earn in a week with 6 visits and 48 miles driven? Enter the amount in dollars, to the nearest cent.

tr.32.16: Calculated the mileage pay but not the visit pay.
tr.1060.02: Swapped the values, using 48 visits and 6 miles.

q: Solve for x: 5x - 9 = 26.
w: Add 9 to both sides: 5x = 35. Divide both sides by 5: x = 7. Check: 5(7) - 9 = 35 - 9 = 26.

n.0: This divides 26 by 5 but leaves the -9 undivided, giving x - 9 = 5.2. Move the 9 first, then divide.
n.1: This stops after adding 9 to both sides; 5x = 35 still has to be divided by 5.
n.2: Sign error: 9 was subtracted from 26 instead of added, giving 5x = 17.

q: Solve for x: 4(x - 3) = 2x + 10.
w: Distribute: 4x - 12 = 2x + 10. Subtract 2x from both sides: 2x - 12 = 10. Add 12: 2x = 22. Divide by 2: x = 11. Check: 4(8) = 32 and 2(11) + 10 = 32.

n.0: This distributes the 4 to x only, giving 4x - 3 = 2x + 10, so 2x = 13.
n.1: Sign error when moving the constant: 4x - 12 = 2x + 10 gives 2x = 22, not 2x = -2.
n.3: This adds 2x to the left side instead of subtracting it, giving 6x - 12 = 10, so 6x = 22.

q: A phlebotomist earns $27.50 per hour plus a flat $165 weekly bonus. Her pay for one week was $1,210, so 27.5h + 165 = 1,210. How many hours, h, did she work that week? Enter the number of hours.

tr.44: Divided 1,210 by 27.50 without first subtracting the $165 bonus.
tr.50: Added the bonus to 1,210 instead of subtracting it.

w: Subtract the bonus from both sides: 27.5h = 1,210 - 165 = 1,045. Divide by 27.5: h = 1,045 ÷ 27.5 = 38 hours. Check: 27.5 × 38 = 1,045, and 1,045 + 165 = 1,210.

q: Solve for x: x/6 + 4 = 11.
w: Subtract 4 from both sides: x/6 = 7. Multiply both sides by 6: x = 42. Check: 42/6 + 4 = 7 + 4 = 11.

n.0: Sign error: 4 was added to 11 instead of subtracted, giving x/6 = 15.
n.1: This divides by 6 instead of multiplying. To undo x/6, multiply both sides by 6.
n.3: This multiplies 11 by 6 but not the 4. Multiplying every term by 6 gives x + 24 = 66, so x = 42.

q: A clinic uses the formula B = 703w / h² to calculate body mass index, where w is weight in pounds and h is height in inches. Which equation gives w in terms of B and h?
w: Multiply both sides by h²: Bh² = 703w. Divide both sides by 703: w = Bh²/703.

n.0: This multiplies by 703 instead of dividing. 703 multiplies w in the formula, so dividing by 703 undoes it.
n.1: This divides by h² instead of multiplying. h² is a divisor in the formula, so multiplying by h² undoes it.
n.3: This leaves 703 in the numerator and h² in the denominator. To isolate w, multiply both sides by h² and divide both sides by 703.

q: Solve for x: -3(2x + 5) = 21.
w: Distribute: -6x - 15 = 21. Add 15 to both sides: -6x = 36. Divide by -6: x = -6. Check: -3(2(-6) + 5) = -3(-7) = 21.

n.1: Sign error in the last step: -6x = 36 gives x = 36 ÷ (-6), which is negative.
n.2: This multiplies only the 2x by -3, giving -6x + 5 = 21, so -6x = 16.
n.3: This subtracts 15 instead of adding it: -6x - 15 = 21 gives -6x = 36, not -6x = 6.

q: An IV bag holds 1,000 mL. It infuses at a constant rate of r mL per hour, and after 8 hours, 280 mL remain in the bag. The equation 1,000 - 8r = 280 models the situation. What is r?
w: 1,000 - 8r = 280. Subtract 1,000 from both sides: -8r = -720. Divide by -8: r = 90 mL per hour. Check: 8 × 90 = 720 mL infused, and 1,000 - 720 = 280 mL left.

n.0: Sign error: this adds 280 to 1,000, giving 8r = 1,280. The 280 mL left must be subtracted from 1,000.
n.1: This divides the amount remaining by 8 hours. The rate comes from the amount infused, 720 mL.
n.3: This divides the full 1,000 mL by 8 hours, as if the bag had emptied.

q: Solve for x: 3(x + 4) - 2x = 19.
w: Distribute: 3x + 12 - 2x = 19. Combine like terms: x + 12 = 19. Subtract 12: x = 7. Check: 3(11) - 14 = 33 - 14 = 19.

n.1: Sign error: 12 was added to 19 instead of subtracted.
n.2: This distributes the 3 to x only, giving 3x + 4 - 2x = 19, so x = 15.
n.3: This adds the 2x instead of subtracting it, giving 5x + 12 = 19, so 5x = 7.

q: Which value of n makes the equation 6n - 4(n - 2) = 30 true?
w: Distribute: 6n - 4n + 8 = 30. Combine like terms: 2n + 8 = 30. Subtract 8: 2n = 22. Divide by 2: n = 11. Check: 66 - 4(9) = 66 - 36 = 30.

n.0: This adds 6n and 4n instead of subtracting, giving 10n + 8 = 30.
n.2: This distributes the -4 to n only, giving 6n - 4n - 2 = 30, so 2n = 32.
n.3: Sign error: -4 × (-2) = +8, but this uses -8, giving 2n - 8 = 30.

q: Solve for x: (3/4)x - 5 = 13.
w: Add 5 to both sides: (3/4)x = 18. Multiply both sides by the reciprocal 4/3: x = 18 × 4/3 = 24. Check: (3/4)(24) - 5 = 18 - 5 = 13.

n.0: This multiplies 18 by 3/4 instead of by its reciprocal, 4/3.
n.2: This multiplies 18 by 4 but does not divide by 3. Multiplying by 4/3 does both.
n.3: Sign error: 5 was subtracted from 13 instead of added, giving (3/4)x = 8.

w: Subtract 0.25x from both sides: 3.5 = 0.5x - 1.5. Add 1.5: 5 = 0.5x. Divide by 0.5: x = 10. Check: 2.5 + 3.5 = 6 and 7.5 - 1.5 = 6.

n.1: This adds 0.25x to 0.75x instead of subtracting it, leaving 1x = 5.
n.2: This multiplies 5 by 0.5 instead of dividing 5 by 0.5.
n.3: Sign error when moving -1.5: adding 1.5 to both sides gives 3.5 + 1.5 = 5, not 3.5 - 1.5 = 2.

q: Solve for x: x/3 + x/4 = 14.
w: Multiply every term by the LCD, 12: 4x + 3x = 168. Combine: 7x = 168. Divide by 7: x = 24. Check: 24/3 + 24/4 = 8 + 6 = 14.

n.1: This adds the numerators and the denominators, treating the sum as 2x/7.
n.2: This multiplies the left side by 12 but not the right side, giving 7x = 14. Every term must be multiplied by 12.
n.3: This adds the denominators, treating x/3 + x/4 as x/7. With a common denominator, 4x/12 + 3x/12 = 7x/12.

q: Solve for x: 5(x - 2) = 3(x + 4).
w: Distribute: 5x - 10 = 3x + 12. Subtract 3x: 2x - 10 = 12. Add 10: 2x = 22. Divide by 2: x = 11. Check: 5(9) = 45 and 3(15) = 45.

n.0: Sign error when moving -10: the right side becomes 12 + 10 = 22, not 12 - 10 = 2.
n.1: This adds 3x to the left side instead of subtracting it, giving 8x - 10 = 12, so 8x = 22.
n.2: This distributes to the x terms only, giving 5x - 2 = 3x + 4, so 2x = 6.

q: Solve for x: 1.2(x + 5) = 0.8x + 10.
w: Distribute: 1.2x + 6 = 0.8x + 10. Subtract 0.8x: 0.4x + 6 = 10. Subtract 6: 0.4x = 4. Divide by 0.4: x = 10. Check: 1.2(15) = 18 and 8 + 10 = 18.

n.1: Sign error: 6 was added to 10 instead of subtracted, giving 0.4x = 16.
n.2: This multiplies only x by 1.2, giving 1.2x + 5 = 0.8x + 10, so 0.4x = 5.
n.3: This adds 0.8x to the left side instead of subtracting it, giving 2x + 6 = 10.

q: Solve for x: (x + 3)/5 = (x - 1)/3.
w: Cross-multiply: 3(x + 3) = 5(x - 1). Distribute: 3x + 9 = 5x - 5. Subtract 3x and add 5: 14 = 2x, so x = 7. Check: 10/5 = 2 and 6/3 = 2.

n.0: This cross-multiplies without distributing: 3x + 3 = 5x - 1 instead of 3(x + 3) = 5(x - 1).
n.2: Sign error in the last step: -2x = -14 gives a positive x.
n.3: This distributes on the left but not on the right: 3x + 9 = 5x - 1.

q: The formula C = (5/9)(F - 32) converts a temperature in degrees Fahrenheit to degrees Celsius. Which equation correctly solves this formula for F?
w: Multiply both sides by 9/5: (9/5)C = F - 32. Add 32 to both sides: F = (9/5)C + 32.

n.0: Sign error: (9/5)C = F - 32, so 32 is added to both sides, not subtracted.
n.1: This adds 32 before multiplying. After multiplying by 9/5 the equation is (9/5)C = F - 32, so 32 is added last.
n.2: This keeps the 5/9. To undo multiplying by 5/9, multiply both sides by its reciprocal, 9/5.

q: Marcus's phone plan costs $35 per month plus $0.10 for each text message over 200. His bill for March was $47.40. How many text messages did he send in March?
w: Let t = texts over 200: 35 + 0.10t = 47.40, so 0.10t = 12.40 and t = 124. Total texts sent = 200 + 124 = 324.

n.1: This subtracts the extra texts from 200 instead of adding them to 200.
n.2: This is the number of texts over the 200 included texts. The total sent is 200 + 124 = 324.
n.3: This divides the whole $47.40 bill by $0.10 without first removing the $35 monthly charge.

q: A pharmacy charges a monthly delivery fee of $12 plus $1.75 for each delivery. A patient's statement shows $54 in delivery charges for the month. How many deliveries did the patient receive? Enter the number of deliveries.

tr.42: Subtracted the $12 fee but did not divide by the $1.75 rate.
tr.37.71: Divided by 1.75 after adding the $12 fee instead of subtracting it.

w: Set up 1.75d + 12 = 54. Subtract 12: 1.75d = 42. Divide by 1.75: d = 24 deliveries. Check: 1.75 × 24 = 42, and 42 + 12 = 54.

q: Gym A charges a $30 joining fee plus $25 per month. Gym B charges a $90 joining fee plus $19 per month. For the number of months at which the total costs of the two gyms are equal, what is that total cost?
w: Set the totals equal: 30 + 25m = 90 + 19m. Subtract 19m and 30 from both sides: 6m = 60, so m = 10 months. Total: 30 + 25(10) = $280. Check Gym B: 90 + 19(10) = $280.

n.0: This is Gym A's monthly charges for 10 months without the $30 joining fee.
n.1: This mixes the plans: Gym B's $90 fee with Gym A's $25 monthly rate for 10 months.
n.2: This adds the fees instead of subtracting them, giving 6m = 120 and m = 20 months, then 30 + 25(20) = $530.

q: Jasmine spent 1/4 of her paycheck on rent and 1/3 of her paycheck on groceries. She had $350 left. What was the amount of her paycheck?

n.0: This treats $350 as 1/3 of the paycheck. The amount left is 5/12 of the paycheck.
n.2: This adds the fractions as 1/4 + 1/3 = 2/7, leaving 5/7. The correct sum is 3/12 + 4/12 = 7/12.
n.3: This divides $350 by 7/12, the fraction she spent. The $350 is the fraction left over, 5/12.

q: In a nursing cohort, two-thirds of the students plus 8 more students equals three-fourths of the cohort. How many students are in the cohort? Enter the number of students.

tr.8: Found that 8 students equal 1/12 of the cohort but did not multiply by 12.

w: Write (2/3)x + 8 = (3/4)x. Multiply every term by 12: 8x + 96 = 9x. Subtract 8x: x = 96. Check: (2/3)(96) = 64, 64 + 8 = 72, and (3/4)(96) = 72.

q: Plan A costs $45 per month plus $0.05 per text message. Plan B costs $30 per month plus $0.10 per text message. For what number of texts in a month do the two plans cost the same?
w: Set the costs equal: 45 + 0.05t = 30 + 0.10t. Subtract 0.05t and 30: 15 = 0.05t, so t = 300 texts. Check: 45 + 15 = $60 and 30 + 30 = $60.

n.1: This adds the per-text rates (0.15) instead of subtracting them.
n.2: This adds the monthly charges ($75) instead of subtracting them.
n.3: This divides the $15 difference by Plan B's rate alone instead of by the 0.05 difference in rates.

q: Three patients are in consecutive even-numbered rooms. The sum of the three room numbers is 642. What is the lowest of the three room numbers?
w: Let the rooms be n, n + 2, and n + 4. Then 3n + 6 = 642, so 3n = 636 and n = 212. Check: 212 + 214 + 216 = 642.

n.0: This is the middle room number (642 ÷ 3), not the lowest.
n.1: This is the highest of the three room numbers.
n.2: This uses consecutive integers (n, n + 1, n + 2), giving 3n + 3 = 642. Consecutive even numbers differ by 2.

q: Jada and Luis split $1,260 in tutoring income. Jada receives $180 more than twice Luis's share. How much does Luis receive?
w: Let L = Luis's share, so Jada's is 2L + 180. Then L + 2L + 180 = 1,260, so 3L = 1,080 and L = $360. Jada gets 2(360) + 180 = $900; 360 + 900 = 1,260.

n.0: This is Jada's share, not Luis's.
n.1: This adds the $180 to $1,260 instead of subtracting it, giving 3L = 1,440.
n.3: This divides $1,080 by 2 instead of by 3. Luis's share counts once and Jada's contains it twice, so there are 3 shares.

q: A tutoring center charges $25 per session for the first 4 sessions and $20 for each session after that. Which expression gives the total cost, in dollars, of n sessions when n is greater than 4?

n.0: This charges for the sessions after the fourth and leaves out the $100 for the first 4.
n.1: This adds $100 for the first 4 sessions but also charges $20 for those same 4 sessions; the $20 rate applies to n - 4 sessions.
n.2: This charges $25 for every session and then charges again for the sessions after the fourth.
